comments.author: @ernestog1620
comments.text: I'm a Software Engineer with over 20 years of experience. While routine development tasks may account for 95% of the coding effort, the true complexity lies in activities such as specification, integration, testing, modular architecture, and component orchestration. These responsibilities often fall on a single individual or a small team, increasing the overhead needed to manage projects effectively. The pace of progress and improvement is directly proportional to the complexity of the final product. Conversely, as reliance on AI for basic coding tasks increases, the time and effort required to deliver a complete, functional solution also rise. It results in more work, not less, within the same human timeframe. This shift demands skills beyond traditional software engineering—particularly a deep understanding of the underlying technology and production code. Only then can developers ask the right questions of the AI. While this might come more naturally to experienced engineers, it presents a significant challenge for those building simpler software solutions without a strong technical foundation.

comments.text:
Just FYI the Tesla full self driving is really just remote controlled driving, just like Waymo. That was the only way the lawmakers would allow Tesla to implement their full self driving taxi service.
The Salesforce CEO (along with several big-tech CEO's that are following suit with layoffs) are idiots. They are trading long-term position for short term gains. AI is a force multiplier. These idiots are looking at it and saying "ooh, I can get the same amount of work done with 30% fewer employees. Lay them off!" Meanwhile, their smarter competitors will be looking at the same data and saying "We're not #1 yet, but #1 is laying off employees. Let's maintain current levels (or even increase them) and use that force multiplier to fly past them."
As for what new developer students should do, I'd say stay in school. Nobody really knows what's going to happen job / salary wise, but one thing is clear: humans will continue coding for decades at least. Now that doesn't mean you'll be earning a 6 figure salary, or that it will even be a good salary. It just means you'll still have a job. My educated guess as to what will happen (as a coder of about 40yrs) is that demand for software will increase as the cost to produce it decreases. Companies will get smaller and coders might even become a gig-economy style job. Until we get sentient AI, human coders will always be needed and I don't mean anyone off the street. You'll need to have all the meta skills at the minimum: critical thinking skills, deductive reasoning, problem solving, UI design concepts, UX concepts, etc. The average Joe off the street isn't going to have this, so the apps they make would be crap on a stick compared to what you will be able to make as a professional.
